summary: Defines a base set of syntaxes and matching rules for LDAP attributes. Syntaxes constrain how values look; matching rules tell the server how to compare values. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: LDAP needs shared rules for how attribute values are written and compared. RFC 4517 defines common value formats and the rules a directory uses to decide whether values match.

questions: what is an ldap matching rule
what is the directory string syntax
subtitle: The base value formats and comparison rules used to define LDAP directory attributes.

tldr.problem: LDAP attributes need shared rules for the format of their values and for comparing those values. A format alone does not say whether two values are equal or how they should be ordered.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4517 defines a base set of syntaxes and matching rules. Each syntax describes a value's structure and LDAP representation; each matching rule defines how an assertion is compared with an attribute value.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is part of the LDAP technical specification. It obsoletes RFC 2252 and RFC 2256 and updates RFC 3698.

today: RFC 4517 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006. It obsoletes RFC 2252 and RFC 2256, and updates RFC 3698.

sections.title: Formats and Comparisons Are Separate
sections.content:
An LDAP attribute has a syntax, which constrains the structure and format of its values. The syntax does not define how two values are compared. A separate matching rule provides that comparison, and its assertion value also has a defined syntax.

RFC 4517 defines a base set of syntaxes and matching rules used when defining LDAP directory attributes. It is part of the LDAP technical specification in RFC 4510. This document obsoletes RFC 2252 and RFC 2256 and updates RFC 3698.
sections.plainLanguage: A syntax says what form an attribute value must have. A matching rule separately says how a server compares that value with a search value.

sections.title: How a Matching Rule Uses a Syntax
sections.content:
An attribute type can name matching rules for equality, ordering and substring comparisons. Each matching rule specifies which attribute syntaxes it applies to, the syntax of its assertion value and a unique object identifier. A rule returns TRUE, FALSE or, in some cases, Undefined.

For character-string rules, RFC 4517 uses the string-preparation procedures in RFC 4518 before comparison. Rules such as caseExactMatch and caseIgnoreMatch differ in whether the preparation step folds letter case. The same stored syntax can therefore support different comparison behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory applies a named rule to compare a stored value with a search value. Some rules distinguish uppercase and lowercase letters; others treat them as equivalent.

sections.title: LDAP Encodings and Object Identifiers
sections.content:
Each syntax defines how its values are represented when transferred in LDAP. These LDAP-specific encodings are octet-aligned and are generally designed to produce character strings that clients can display. A client must not assume an unrecognized syntax is readable text; JPEG data is one example that is not reasonably represented as readable text.

Each syntax has a unique dotted-decimal object identifier. A definition may include a suggested upper length bound in curly braces. Such a bound is not part of the syntax identifier, and a character count may differ from an octet count because UTF-8 uses variable-length encodings.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAP gives each value format a numeric identifier and a transfer representation. The representation may be readable text, but a client cannot assume that for a format it does not recognize.

sections.title: Examples of the Defined Syntaxes
sections.content:
The syntax set covers values such as Boolean, Integer, Bit String, Country String, IA5 String, Octet String, OID, JPEG, telephone number and directory-specific schema descriptions. Directory String contains one or more characters from the Universal Character Set and is encoded as UTF-8. Servers and clients must be prepared for arbitrary code points, including ones that are not printable ASCII.

The DN syntax represents a distinguished name using the string form in RFC 4514. Generalized Time represents a date and time using a restricted ISO 8601 format; the RFC says the UTC Z form should be preferred to a time-zone differential. The definitions also include string formats for postal addresses, numeric strings and other directory values.
sections.plainLanguage: The syntax list includes common values such as yes-or-no, whole numbers, text, addresses and times. Each definition also gives the form used to transfer that value through LDAP.

sections.title: Equality, Ordering and Substring Rules
sections.content:
The matching rules cover several kinds of comparisons. Equality rules can compare integers, booleans, object identifiers, distinguished names, times or strings. Ordering rules determine whether one value comes before another, and substring rules check whether ordered pieces appear within a value.

For Directory String, caseExactMatch compares prepared characters without folding case, while caseIgnoreMatch folds case during preparation. A substring rule can also require an initial or final piece to match the corresponding end of the value. Servers should implement the listed rules other than wordMatch and keywordMatch, which they may implement.
sections.plainLanguage: Matching rules let a search ask whether values are equal, ordered or contain specified text. The rule determines details such as whether letter case matters.

sections.title: What LDAP Servers Must Publish
sections.content:
Servers should recognize all syntaxes listed in the RFC, although recognition does not require full support. Servers may recognize additional syntaxes, but the RFC discourages arbitrary additions because clients may not understand them.

Servers must publish definitions of matching rules referenced by attribute-type and matching-rule-use definitions in the same subschema entry. A server that implements the extensibleMatch filter should allow the listed rules in that filter when their assertion syntax matches the attribute value syntax. RFC 4517 also updates the IANA LDAP descriptors registry with the defined matching-rule names and identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: A server should recognize the standard formats and most standard comparison rules. It must publish the matching-rule definitions that its schema uses so clients can discover them.

sections.title: Canonical Forms and Security-Sensitive Comparisons
sections.content:
LDAP-specific encodings are not always canonical. Converting a value to another encoding and back may not reproduce the original octets. The RFC therefore says not to use these encodings where a canonical encoding or reversibility to DER is required, such as when verifying digital signatures.

When implementations interpret security-sensitive fields, especially fields that grant or deny access, they must compare the underlying abstract value regardless of the encoding used. This prevents different representations of the same value from producing different access decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: One value can have different valid encodings, so the written bytes are not always a reliable basis for a security decision. Compare the value's meaning when deciding whether to grant or deny access.
